passages.happening:
The king and Haman come to Esther's second banquet, and as they drink their wine the king asks a third time: “Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be fulfilled” (verse 2).

This time she answers. “If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it pleases the king, grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request” (verse 3). ‘For my people and I have been sold out to destruction, death, and annihilation’ (verse 4). If they had only been sold as slaves, she says, she would have kept silent.

The king asks, “Who is this, and where is the one who would devise such a scheme?” (verse 5). Esther names him: “The adversary and enemy is this wicked man” (verse 6), Haman. ‘And Haman stood in terror before the king and queen’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The suspense Esther built in chapter 5 now breaks.

Her plea is carefully framed. She speaks first of her own life and then of her people's. She uses the words of Haman's own decree, destruction, death and annihilation. And she uses the word sold, which turns Haman's offer of silver to the treasury into what it really was: the purchase of a people's death.

Haman had asked to destroy an unnamed people whose laws were different. The king now learns that this people includes his own queen. Whether he had grasped what he agreed to before is not clear, and the narrator shows him more stung by the insult to himself than moved by the fate of a people.

Esther names Haman the adversary and the enemy. From now on the book calls him the enemy of the Jews.
passages.later: The words Esther throws back at the king are the words of Haman's decree: ‘to destroy, kill, and annihilate all the Jews’ (3:13). Joseph's brothers once sold a brother into slavery (Genesis 37:28); here a whole people has been sold to death.
passages.asks: Esther named herself with her people, and then she named the enemy. Ask whether there is someone you need to stand beside openly, at a cost to yourself. And ask what wrong you have seen that needs to be named plainly, to the one who can stop it.

passages.happening:
‘In his fury, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden, while Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he realized that the king was planning a terrible fate for him’ (verse 7).

As the king comes back, Haman is falling on the couch where Esther is reclining. The king cries out, “Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?” (verse 8), and Haman's face is covered.

Harbonah, one of the king's eunuchs, says, “There is a gallows fifty cubits high at Haman’s house. He had it built for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king” (verse 9). The king orders Haman hanged on it. ‘So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the fury of the king subsided’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
At a Persian banquet, guests reclined on couches. That explains verse 8: Haman, pleading for his life, falls onto the couch where Esther lies just as the king returns. Court rules strictly limited contact between men and the king's women, and even coming this close to the queen could be read as a grave offense. The king's charge may be a deliberate misreading, but in that world it sealed Haman's fate.

The covering of Haman's face is not explained. Many take it as a sign of condemnation; others think of shame. Either way, it marks the moment Haman is finished.

The book has been building to this. Haman's advisers said he would fall before Mordecai, and now he literally falls. The man who built a gallows for an innocent man dies on it. The chapter tells it briefly and does not linger.

Haman is dead, but his decree still stands. The Jews of the empire are still marked for the thirteenth of Adar, and chapter 8 must deal with that.
passages.later: The psalms describe the same turn: ‘He has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making’ (Psalm 7:15). And Proverbs says, ‘He who digs a pit will fall into it’ (Proverbs 26:27).
passages.hard:
Is Esther cruel to let Haman die when he begs her for his life?

Some readers are troubled that Esther says nothing when Haman falls before her pleading, and that the story seems to delight in his downfall. It helps to remember what Haman had done. He had arranged the killing of every Jew in the empire, children included, and he had built a gallows for Mordecai the day before. His plea came only once he was exposed, not from repentance.

The decision to execute him belonged to the king, and nothing suggests that Esther had the power to overrule a furious Persian king, or that sparing Haman would have removed the decree that still threatened her people. The narrator reports without comment. Elsewhere the Bible calls believers to love their enemies and to leave vengeance to God, and it also affirms that those who govern may justly punish grave wrongdoing. The book records a judgment; it does not invite anyone to take revenge.
passages.asks: Haman built the gallows that ended his own life. Ask whether a plan you are making against someone else might turn back on you. And ask how you can leave judgment to God instead of taking it into your own hands.
